title: Chapter 2 Drill: Fluids, Electrolytes, Acid-Base Balance, and Nutrition

items.stem: Four years after a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, a 50-year-old woman has progressive gait unsteadiness, numbness in the legs, anemia, and low white cell count. Her vitamin B12 and folate are normal. Which deficiency should be checked next?
options: Copper, which impairs the spinal cord and bone marrow and can mimic B12 deficiency
Vitamin C, which causes bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhage, and poor wound healing
Vitamin D, which causes bone pain but not myelopathy
Vitamin A, which causes night blindness and dry eyes
items.explanation: Copper is absorbed in the proximal stomach and duodenum, which a bypass excludes, so deficiency can develop years later. It causes a myeloneuropathy resembling subacute combined degeneration, with anemia and neutropenia, despite normal B12 levels. Zinc excess from supplements may contribute. Vitamin D, C, and A deficiencies have different clinical features. Treatment is copper replacement, intravenously if the deficiency is severe.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease who missed dialysis presents before urgent hernia repair with a potassium of 7.1 mEq/L and widened QRS complexes. He has received intravenous calcium and the ECG is improving. Which is the best next step to lower serum potassium quickly?
options: A single dose of sodium polystyrene as the only measure, given by mouth right now
A saline infusion alone to dilute the potassium
Regular insulin with dextrose, plus nebulized albuterol, while arranging dialysis
Intravenous potassium-free fluid with no other treatment
items.explanation: After membrane stabilization with calcium, potassium is driven into cells with insulin plus glucose and inhaled beta agonists, which act within minutes but are temporary. Definitive removal requires dialysis in a patient with kidney failure, or diuretics, binders, or both when function remains. Binders alone act too slowly for an unstable rhythm, and fluid dilution is ineffective and unsafe in anuria. Glucose is monitored because insulin can cause hypoglycemia.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman is two months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and is taking a daily calcium supplement and vitamin D. She asks which calcium form is best absorbed after her operation. What should be recommended?
options: Calcium citrate, because it does not require stomach acid for absorption
Calcium carbonate, because it is better absorbed without gastric acid
No calcium, because the bypass increases calcium absorption
Calcium taken together with a proton pump inhibitor
items.explanation: After bypass, the stomach pouch produces little acid and the duodenum, where calcium is mainly absorbed, is bypassed, so calcium citrate, which dissolves without acid, is preferred over carbonate. Patients need lifelong supplementation with vitamin D to prevent metabolic bone disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Acid suppression further lowers carbonate absorption, and bypass does not enhance calcium uptake. Doses are split, since absorption is limited at each time.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man with a high-output pancreatic fistula after distal pancreatectomy loses several liters per day. His laboratory results show sodium 138, chloride 112, bicarbonate 16 mEq/L, and a calculated anion gap of 10. What best explains his acid-base disorder?
options: Anion gap metabolic acidosis from accumulating lactate and poor tissue perfusion
Metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid
Respiratory acidosis from impaired ventilation
Non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from loss of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic fluid
items.explanation: Pancreatic secretions are rich in bicarbonate, so a high-output fistula or diarrhea produces a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap, because chloride rises to replace lost bicarbonate. His gap of 10 is normal, which argues against lactate or other unmeasured acids. Gastric loss would produce alkalosis, and ventilation problems would affect carbon dioxide. Treatment replaces losses with a bicarbonate or lactate-containing solution and reduces output.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a serum ionized calcium of 0.85 mmol/L after total thyroidectomy. Which ECG finding is most characteristic of her electrolyte abnormality?
options: Peaked T waves with a widened QRS complex
Prolongation of the QT interval
Shortening of the QT interval
Prominent U waves with flattened T waves
items.explanation: Hypocalcemia prolongs the plateau phase of the cardiac action potential and so lengthens the ST segment and QT interval, which predisposes to torsades de pointes. Hypercalcemia shortens the QT interval. Peaked T waves and a wide QRS characterize hyperkalemia, and U waves with flat T waves characterize hypokalemia. Neuromuscular signs, such as perioral paresthesia and Chvostek and Trousseau signs, accompany the ECG change.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man in septic shock has an arterial pH of 7.18, a bicarbonate of 12 mEq/L, and a carbon dioxide tension of 40 mm Hg. Using the Winter formula, what does the carbon dioxide level indicate?
options: Appropriate respiratory compensation for the metabolic acidosis
A coexisting respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation
A coexisting respiratory acidosis, because expected compensation would be near 26 mm Hg
A pure metabolic acidosis with no respiratory contribution
items.explanation: The Winter formula predicts the expected carbon dioxide tension as 1.5 times the bicarbonate plus 8, with a range of 2 either way, so a bicarbonate of 12 predicts about 26 mm Hg. A measured level of 40 is much higher, indicating inadequate ventilatory compensation and a concomitant respiratory acidosis, often a sign of fatigue and impending respiratory failure. Hyperventilation would produce a value below the predicted range, and appropriate compensation would match the formula.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man with Crohn disease underwent resection of 120 cm of terminal ileum five years ago and now has mild fatigue, a macrocytic anemia, and a low serum cobalamin. What is the best long-term treatment?
options: Lifelong vitamin B12 by injection or high-dose supplementation
A short course of oral iron, since ileal resection causes iron loss
Folate alone, since it corrects all causes of macrocytosis
Dietary changes alone, since stores regenerate within months
items.explanation: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed only in the terminal ileum, so resection of more than roughly 60 cm, or any extensive ileal disease, leads to deficiency that requires lifelong parenteral or high-dose replacement. Folate alone can mask hematologic findings while neurologic damage progresses. Iron is absorbed in the proximal bowel, and dietary adjustment cannot restore absent absorptive surface.

items.stem: On the fourth day after a large laparotomy for peritonitis, a 58-year-old woman has generalized edema but is now hemodynamically stable. Her urine output has risen without diuretics, her weight is falling, and her serum albumin is rising. What does this pattern represent?
options: Acute kidney injury that has progressed to a polyuric phase of acute tubular necrosis
Mobilization of sequestered third-space fluid back into the circulation
Early adrenal insufficiency causing urinary sodium loss
Developing diabetes insipidus from sedative medication
items.explanation: After major surgery or inflammation, a sequestration phase shifts functional extracellular fluid into the interstitium, followed by a mobilization phase after about two to four days, when fluid returns to the circulation and is excreted. Spontaneous diuresis with falling weight in a stable patient signals recovery. More fluid is not needed, and diuretics are used only for overload. The picture does not suggest tubular necrosis, adrenal failure, or diabetes insipidus.

items.stem: A severely malnourished 44-year-old woman has been ventilated for ten days. Parenteral nutrition at full target began three days ago, and now she cannot be weaned, has muscle weakness, and a phosphate of 1.0 mg/dL. What is the best management?
options: Continue full-rate feeding and give a diuretic for weaning
Stop all nutrition for about two weeks to let the electrolyte levels recover fully
Increase glucose delivery to speed anabolism
Replace phosphate intravenously and reduce the caloric rate, then advance slowly
items.explanation: Feeding after prolonged starvation drives insulin release and cellular uptake of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, producing refeeding syndrome with respiratory muscle weakness, arrhythmia, and failure to wean. Treatment is electrolyte replacement and cutting calories to a fraction of the target with a gradual increase, plus thiamine. Stopping nutrition for weeks worsens malnutrition, and more glucose aggravates the shift.

items.stem: A 70 kg man is kept without oral intake after an uncomplicated operation and has no abnormal losses. The team wants to calculate his maintenance fluid rate using the weight-based rule of four, two, and one mL per kilogram per hour. What rate results?
options: About 70 mL per hour, from one mL per kilogram for every hour
About 140 mL per hour, from two mL per kilogram for every hour
About 110 mL per hour
About 280 mL per hour, from four mL per kilogram for every hour
items.explanation: The four-two-one rule gives 4 mL per kilogram per hour for the first 10 kg, 2 mL for the next 10 kg, and 1 mL for each kilogram above 20. For 70 kg this is 40 plus 20 plus 50, or 110 mL per hour. Applying a single factor to the entire weight overestimates or underestimates requirements. Actual orders are then adjusted for ongoing losses, cardiac or renal disease, and the patient's measured volume status.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with hypertension has a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L, a bicarbonate of 34 mEq/L, and a urinary chloride concentration above 40 mEq/L despite no diuretic use or vomiting. A saline infusion does not correct the alkalosis. Which disorder should be suspected?
options: Mineralocorticoid excess such as primary aldosteronism, a chloride-resistant alkalosis
Contraction alkalosis from repeated vomiting and volume depletion in the past week
Alkalosis from chronic nasogastric suction
Post-diuretic alkalosis with low urinary chloride
items.explanation: Metabolic alkalosis is divided by urinary chloride. Low chloride (under about 20 mEq/L) indicates chloride-responsive causes such as vomiting, gastric suction, or remote diuretic use, which correct with saline and potassium. High chloride with hypertension and hypokalemia that is resistant to saline points to mineralocorticoid excess, because aldosterone drives renal hydrogen and potassium loss. Aldosterone and renin testing and imaging would follow.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man in sinus rhythm is ventilated with fixed tidal volumes after a Whipple procedure and has a blood pressure of 88/52 mm Hg. His arterial line shows pulse pressure variation of 18 percent with respiration. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: He is fluid overloaded and should receive a diuretic
Variation of this size excludes hypovolemia as a cause
Only a central venous pressure value can guide fluid therapy
He is likely fluid responsive, and a crystalloid bolus is reasonable
items.explanation: In mechanically ventilated patients in sinus rhythm with adequate tidal volumes, pulse pressure or stroke volume variation above roughly 13 percent predicts that cardiac output will rise with a fluid bolus. Dynamic measures outperform static pressures such as central venous pressure. These indices are unreliable with spontaneous breathing, arrhythmia, or low tidal volume. Large respiratory variation suggests preload dependence, not overload, and does not rule out hypovolemia.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with short bowel syndrome and an intact colon develops episodes of slurred speech, ataxia, and confusion after high-carbohydrate meals. Her anion gap is elevated, but her standard lactate level is normal. What is the best treatment?
options: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion with continued high-sugar feeds
Oral antibiotics to reduce colonic bacteria and a lower carbohydrate diet
Insulin infusion to treat the presumed ketoacidosis
Urgent hemodialysis for suspected toxic ingestion
items.explanation: D-lactic acidosis occurs in short bowel syndrome when unabsorbed carbohydrate reaches colonic bacteria that produce D-lactate, which humans metabolize poorly and which standard assays do not detect. It causes encephalopathy with an elevated anion gap. Treatment is dietary carbohydrate restriction, oral antibiotics to suppress the flora, and correcting dehydration. Bicarbonate alone does not remove the source, and the picture does not suggest ketoacidosis or toxin ingestion.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman who underwent a biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch three years ago reports difficulty seeing in dim light and has steatorrhea. She has missed her fat-soluble vitamin supplements. Which deficiency most likely explains her visual symptom?
options: Vitamin A deficiency from fat malabsorption in a short common channel
Vitamin B1 deficiency from reduced thiamine intake
Vitamin C deficiency from reduced citrus intake
Vitamin B12 deficiency from loss of intrinsic factor
items.explanation: Diversion procedures with a short common channel cause marked fat malabsorption, so the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K become deficient without lifelong supplementation and monitoring. Vitamin A deficiency presents with night blindness and xerophthalmia. Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy and neuropathy, vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, and B12 deficiency causes anemia and neuropathy, so none explains impaired dim-light vision.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with a high-output ileostomy and poor intake develops a scaly rash around his mouth and perineum, hair thinning, diarrhea, and a stalled wound. His albumin is normal. Which deficiency best explains this picture?
options: Vitamin K deficiency, which presents mainly with bleeding
Vitamin C deficiency, which presents with perifollicular hemorrhage
Zinc deficiency, which is increased by large small-bowel losses
Vitamin B12 deficiency, which presents with neuropathy first
items.explanation: Zinc is lost in intestinal secretions, so patients with high-output ostomies, fistulas, or diarrhea are at risk. Deficiency causes acral and periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea, impaired taste, and poor wound healing. Vitamin K deficiency mainly causes coagulopathy, vitamin C deficiency produces scurvy with perifollicular bleeding and gum disease, and B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy. Replacement is oral or intravenous zinc.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has a prolonged ileus after colectomy and a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L with a normal magnesium. She has only peripheral intravenous access and is on cardiac monitoring. What is the maximum usual rate for potassium chloride through a peripheral vein?
options: About 40 mEq per hour, to speed correction in a monitored patient
About 2 mEq per hour, which is the only safe rate
Any rate, because peripheral veins tolerate concentrated solutions
About 10 mEq per hour, with ECG monitoring
items.explanation: Potassium chloride is irritating to veins, and the usual limit is about 10 mEq per hour peripherally, with higher rates of up to about 20 mEq per hour reserved for central lines and monitored settings. Faster infusion risks cardiac arrest and phlebitis. Rates as low as 2 mEq per hour are unnecessarily slow for symptomatic or severe deficiency. Magnesium must also be corrected, since hypomagnesemia perpetuates potassium wasting.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has received 14 units of packed red cells and plasma during damage control surgery for a hepatic injury. She becomes hypotensive with a prolonged QT interval, and her ionized calcium is 0.78 mmol/L. What is the mechanism and treatment?
options: Hyperkalemia from stored cells, so insulin alone is given
Citrate in transfused blood binds calcium, so intravenous calcium is given
Hypermagnesemia from plasma, so a diuretic is given
Hypernatremia from the preservative solution, so free water is given immediately
items.explanation: Stored blood products contain citrate, an anticoagulant that chelates ionized calcium. During massive transfusion, especially with liver dysfunction that slows citrate metabolism, ionized calcium falls, causing hypotension, reduced contractility, and a prolonged QT interval. Treatment is intravenous calcium chloride or gluconate with ionized calcium monitoring. Hyperkalemia can occur with transfusion but produces peaked T waves and a wide QRS rather than a long QT, and sodium and magnesium are not the issue.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman who had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 18 months ago reports episodes of sweating, tremor, and confusion about two hours after eating sweets. Glucose measures 42 mg/dL during an episode. Which mechanism best explains her symptoms?
options: Exaggerated insulin release after rapid carbohydrate absorption, causing late dumping hypoglycemia
An insulin-secreting pancreatic tumor that requires localization and resection
Adrenal insufficiency from nutritional deficiency
Rapid fluid shifts into the bowel that cause early dumping
items.explanation: Late dumping syndrome occurs one to three hours after meals, when rapid delivery of carbohydrate to the small bowel causes a surge in glucose and incretin hormones followed by excessive insulin and reactive hypoglycemia. Early dumping, within about 30 minutes, reflects osmotic fluid shifts and produces cramping, flushing, and diarrhea. Treatment is small low-carbohydrate meals, with acarbose or octreotide if needed, and other causes are considered only if symptoms persist.

items.stem: After transsphenoidal resection of a pituitary adenoma, a 39-year-old man has urine output of 400 mL per hour, a serum sodium of 151 mEq/L, serum osmolality of 318 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality of 90 mOsm/kg. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Fluid restriction with a vasopressin receptor antagonist to concentrate his urine
Desmopressin, with free water replacement guided by serial sodium measurements
Hypertonic saline to correct the polyuria
A loop diuretic to enhance free water excretion
items.explanation: Polyuria with hypernatremia, high serum osmolality, and inappropriately dilute urine after pituitary surgery indicates central diabetes insipidus from loss of antidiuretic hormone. Desmopressin replaces the hormone, and free water is replaced while sodium is monitored. A receptor antagonist or fluid restriction would worsen the hypernatremia, which suits syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis. Hypertonic saline and diuretics raise sodium further.

items.stem: A 74-year-old nursing home resident with pneumonia and poor oral intake has a sodium of 162 mEq/L, dry mucous membranes, and orthostatic hypotension. He has been symptomatic for about a week. What is the best plan for correcting his sodium?
options: Give sterile water by vein quickly until the sodium is normal within a few hours
Give hypertonic saline to replace the lost sodium
Restore volume with isotonic fluid if hypotensive, then replace free water gradually
Restrict all fluids and start a loop diuretic
items.explanation: Hypernatremia from water loss is corrected after first restoring circulating volume with isotonic fluid if the patient is hypotensive, then replacing the free water deficit with hypotonic fluid or enteral water. In chronic hypernatremia, brain cells have adapted, and lowering sodium faster than about 10 to 12 mEq/L per day risks cerebral edema. Hypertonic saline, fluid restriction, and diuretics all worsen the hypertonic, dehydrated state.

items.stem: A critically ill 66-year-old man with respiratory failure and sepsis is being fed enterally. A resident is setting the daily protein target for his nutrition orders. Which range best matches current critical care guidance?
options: About 0.2 to 0.4 grams per kilogram per day
About 3.0 to 4.0 grams per kilogram per day
About 0.8 grams per kilogram per day as for healthy adults
About 1.2 to 2.0 grams per kilogram per day
items.explanation: Critical illness causes intense catabolism and loss of lean mass, and guidelines suggest 1.2 to 2.0 grams of protein per kilogram daily, with higher needs in burns, trauma, and obesity targeted to ideal body weight in some protocols. Healthy adults need about 0.8 gram per kilogram, which underfeeds the critically ill. Doses above about 2.5 grams per kilogram add urea load without clear benefit, and very low intake worsens wasting.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has persistent muscle cramps and a corrected calcium of 6.9 mg/dL four days after a Whipple procedure with prolonged gastric drainage and diuretic use. She has received calcium supplements with little response. Her magnesium is 0.9 mg/dL. What is the best intervention?
options: Increase the oral calcium dose several fold without changing any other part of the regimen
Give vitamin A to improve calcium absorption
Replace magnesium, since hypomagnesemia impairs parathyroid hormone release and action
Begin a thiazide diuretic to increase calcium reabsorption
items.explanation: Severe hypomagnesemia causes functional hypoparathyroidism by impairing the secretion of parathyroid hormone and causing end-organ resistance, so hypocalcemia remains refractory until magnesium is replaced. Thiazides reduce urinary calcium but lower magnesium too, and raising calcium doses cannot overcome the defect. Vitamin D, not vitamin A, aids absorption. Replacement is intravenous in symptomatic or severe deficiency, with caution in kidney failure.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C, tense ascites, and edema is admitted for umbilical hernia complications. His sodium is 122 mEq/L, his urine sodium is low, and he is not confused. What is the best initial management of the hyponatremia?
options: Infuse hypertonic saline quickly to normalize the sodium
Infuse large volumes of isotonic saline to restore his circulating volume quickly
Give a loop diuretic along with unrestricted water intake
Restrict free water and sodium, and hold diuretics if the level is falling
items.explanation: Hypervolemic hyponatremia in cirrhosis reflects excess total body water relative to sodium from nonosmotic vasopressin release. Management is free water restriction, treatment of the underlying disease, and cautious use or holding of diuretics. Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms. Isotonic saline worsens ascites and edema without raising sodium, and unrestricted water perpetuates the problem. Correction should not exceed about 8 mEq/L per day.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man has received parenteral nutrition for three weeks because of an enterocutaneous fistula. His total bilirubin and alanine aminotransferase are rising, and ultrasound shows a steatotic liver without bile duct dilation. What is the best change in management?
options: Increase total calories and lipid to correct the presumed malnutrition and cholestasis
Avoid overfeeding, cycle the infusion, and begin enteral intake as soon as possible
Stop all nutrition and observe the liver tests
Add a long course of broad-spectrum antibiotics
items.explanation: Parenteral nutrition-associated liver disease arises from overfeeding, excess dextrose and lipid, lack of enteral stimulation, and sepsis. Management reduces total calories and lipid dose, cycles the infusion, treats infection, and restores enteral feeding as soon as possible, because gut stimulation promotes bile flow. More calories worsen the process, stopping all nutrition risks starvation, and antibiotics help only when infection is documented.

items.stem: A medical student is estimating the water distribution in a healthy 70 kg man. Total body water is about 60 percent of body weight. Approximately how much of that water lies inside cells?
options: About 28 liters, or two thirds of total body water
About 14 liters, or one third of total body water
About 42 liters, since all body water is inside cells
About 3 liters, matching the plasma volume
items.explanation: Total body water in a 70 kg man is about 42 liters. Two thirds, roughly 28 liters, is intracellular, and one third, about 14 liters, is extracellular. Of the extracellular fluid, about one quarter is plasma (near 3.5 liters) and the rest is interstitial. This distribution explains why isotonic crystalloid expands plasma only modestly, and why free water spreads across all compartments.
